Distributor, reseller or agent: which US route to market fits your product?

Each one carries a different share of the stock, the risk and the customer. The right choice depends on how American buyers expect to buy in your category.

By Taz Abbas, Managing Partner · Published October 28, 2026 · B2B Partnerships

The short answer

Use a distributor when American buyers expect to buy from a local supplier that holds stock, offers credit terms and ships fast. Use a reseller when the sale needs local expertise, such as installation, integration or support. Use a sales agent when you can ship, invoice and support customers yourself and mainly need someone to open doors. Many companies end up with more than one, in a deliberate order.

What each route actually does

The three names get used loosely, so it helps to define them by who carries what.

  • Distributor. Buys your product, holds it in the US, resells it and collects payment from its customers. It carries the inventory and the credit risk, and earns the margin between what it pays you and what it sells for. In many categories a distributor sells mainly to resellers rather than to end customers.
  • Reseller. Buys your product, often through a distributor, and sells it to the end customer, usually together with its own services. A value-added reseller earns a margin on the product and is often paid separately for the work around it.
  • Sales agent. Finds and develops customers for you but does not buy the product. You ship, invoice and collect yourself, and the agent earns a commission on the sales it brings in. You keep the customer relationship and the pricing, and you also keep the logistics and the risk.

Who carries what, side by side

A quick way to compare the routes is to ask who holds each part of the business once a US order arrives.

  • Inventory. The distributor holds it. A reseller may hold a little or order per deal. With an agent, you hold it.
  • Credit and collections. The distributor extends terms to its customers and collects. A reseller collects from the end customer. With an agent, you invoice and chase payment yourself.
  • The customer relationship. It sits furthest from you with a distributor, closer with a reseller and closest with an agent, who introduces you and then steps back.
  • Price control. You set a price to the distributor or reseller, and they set their own resale price. With an agent you quote the customer directly.

The more of these a partner carries, the less of the final price you keep, and the less work and risk you take on. Neither side of that trade is better in itself. It has to fit the stage you are at.

When does a distributor fit?

A distributor fits when availability decides the sale. If your buyers order often, in small quantities, and expect delivery in days from a supplier they already have an account with, a distributor gives you that reach from the first order. It also takes on work that is hard to do from abroad: importing, warehousing, US invoicing and collecting from many small accounts.

The trade-off is distance from the end customer. A distributor carries thousands of products, so yours competes for attention inside its catalog. Plan for the training, marketing support and sales follow-up that make a distributor's team want to sell it. Signing a distributor is the start of the work, not the end of it. The vendors that do well usually have someone on their side who checks in with the distributor's product and sales teams every week.

When does a reseller fit?

A reseller fits when the product does not sell itself. Technology that has to be configured, integrated with other systems or supported locally is usually bought from someone the customer trusts to make it work. The reseller brings that trust and the people to deliver it.

Resellers choose vendors that are easy to sell and profitable to support. Before you recruit them, be ready with clear margins, deal registration or another way to protect their opportunities, product training and a named contact who answers quickly. Think too about what the reseller earns after the first sale. Services, renewals and support contracts often matter more to a reseller than the margin on the product, so show how your product leads to that work.

When does a sales agent fit?

An agent fits when the sale is large, technical or relationship-driven and the number of buyers is small enough to serve directly. If you can already ship to the US, invoice in dollars and support customers from where you are, an agent adds market knowledge and introductions without adding a layer between you and the customer.

Agents work on commission, so they favour products that close in a reasonable time. Agree in writing which territory and accounts they cover, how commission is earned and when it is paid. Several US states have laws on paying sales representatives, which is one reason to have the agreement checked locally.

Can you use more than one route?

Yes, and many vendors do. A common pattern in the US is two-tier distribution: a distributor holds stock and extends credit, and resellers buy from it and sell to the end customer. Another is to start with an agent or a few direct accounts to prove demand, then add distribution once volume justifies it.

What causes trouble is overlap nobody planned. If a distributor, a reseller and your own team all quote the same customer, prices fall and partners lose trust. Decide early who owns which customers, regions or deal sizes, and write it down.

Signs the route is not working

Give any new route a fair run, then look for these signals:

  • Stock sits with the distributor and reorders do not come.
  • Resellers register deals but rarely close them, or stop registering at all.
  • The agent sends introductions that never turn into qualified opportunities.
  • Partners ask for deeper discounts on every deal to make the product worth their time.
  • Customers contact you directly because the partner could not answer their questions.

Each one points to a different fix. It may be more training, better margins, clearer rules on who owns a deal, or a different route altogether. Find the cause before you change partners, because a new partner on the same terms tends to hit the same problem.

Questions to answer before you choose

  1. How do buyers in your category buy today, and from whom?
  2. Does the product need installation, integration or local support?
  3. How much margin can you give up at each step and still make money?
  4. How much control do you need over price, brand and the customer relationship?
  5. Can you handle US importing, invoicing, collections and returns yourself?
  6. How fast do you need sales, and how much can you invest before they come?

The answers usually point to one route as the place to start. If they point in different directions, that is a sign to research the market more closely before signing anyone. Talking to a handful of buyers and the partners they already use is often the fastest way to settle it.

A note on agreements

Whichever route you choose, the agreement shapes the relationship for years. Pay attention to exclusivity, territory, minimum commitments, pricing, who owns the customer data and how either side can end the arrangement. Laws differ between states, so have a US lawyer look at the agreement before you sign. This post is general guidance, not legal advice.
